title: Stuart Broad Calls Pakistan 'a Poor Side,' Predicts England 3-0 Sweep
excerpt: The former England fast bowler delivers a blunt verdict as Pakistan struggle at Headingley, trailing by 195 runs after being bowled out for 171.
body:
• Former England fast bowler Stuart Broad has called Pakistan "a poor side" and predicted England will win the three-Test series 3-0.
  • Pakistan were bowled out for 171 on Day 1 at Headingley, with Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue taking five wickets apiece.
  • England built a 195-run first-innings lead through half-centuries from Joe Root (66), Jordan Cox (73), Harry Brook (91), and Dan Lawrence (51).
  • Pakistan have lost 13 of their last 18 Tests and last won a Test in England eight years ago.

Broad Delivers Blunt Assessment

Former England fast bowler Stuart Broad has delivered a withering verdict on Pakistan's Test team, describing them as "a poor side" and backing England to complete a comfortable 3-0 clean sweep in the ongoing three-Test series.

Speaking on The Love for Cricket Podcast after the first two days of the opening Test at Headingley, Broad was unsparing in his assessment of a Pakistan side that has now lost 13 of its last 18 Tests.

"They are a poor side, they are not a really good side. You would imagine and you'd think that England should win 3-0. And pretty comfortably."

— Stuart Broad, former England fast bowler

Broad, who took 604 Test wickets in a career spanning 17 years, acknowledged that a clean sweep could not be taken for granted but said failure to win the series would be a "huge failure" for England.

England Dominate at Headingley

The opening Test has underlined Broad's assessment. Joe Root won the toss and inserted Pakistan on a pitch offering seam movement, and his bowlers responded emphatically. Ollie Robinson, returning from a knee injury, trapped Azan Awais lbw with the very first ball of the series — the first time a wicket had fallen to the first delivery of a series in England.

Robinson finished with 5-51, removing four of Pakistan's top five, while Josh Tongue's pace accounted for the tail as he returned 5-46. Pakistan were bowled out for 171, with only Abdullah Shafique's 61 providing meaningful resistance. A 91-run partnership between Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq (42) briefly steadied the innings before five wickets tumbled for just 21 runs.

England's batting then piled on the pressure. Root, captaining again after Ben Stokes's retirement, made 66 and shared a 150-run stand with Jordan Cox, who scored 73 on his first outing at number three — deputizing for the injured Jacob Bethell. Harry Brook, the world's top-ranked Test batter, narrowly missed a century at his home ground, falling for 91 from 93 balls. Dan Lawrence contributed 51 on his return to Test cricket after two years away.

Pakistan's Lone Bright Spot

Left-arm spinner Ali Usman provided Pakistan's only real positive, claiming 5-92 for his maiden Test five-wicket haul. His arm-ball accounted for Brook and successive dismissals of Gus Atkinson and Robinson sealed his milestone. It was the first five-wicket haul by a visiting spinner at Headingley since Australia's Ashley Mallett in the 1972 Ashes.

But Usman's effort came against a backdrop of indisciplined seam bowling and poor ground fielding that gifted England easy runs. Brook was dropped on one at second slip by stand-in captain Salman Ali Agha — a miss that proved devastatingly costly.

England closed Day 2 on 366-8, a lead of 195 runs with better weather forecast for the remaining three days. Pakistan, who last won a Test in England eight years ago, face a steep uphill battle to prevent England from seizing a decisive lead in the series.

A Crisis Running Deep

Pakistan's struggles in England are part of a broader malaise. The team has been on a downward trajectory since a record defeat in the Multan Test last year, when they became the first team to suffer an innings defeat after posting more than 500 in the first innings. The bowling attack, once spearheaded by the likes of Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis, and Shoaib Akhtar, now lacks the firepower to trouble top batting lineups in seam-friendly conditions.

For the millions of Pakistani cricket fans in the diaspora — particularly the large communities in England — the series offers a painful watch. With the keel-laying ceremony at Headingley barely complete, this first Test appears headed toward a decisive English victory.
